paper_context.research_question: Can simple sequence LSTM models augmented with linguistically motivated regularizers (for sentiment lexicon entries, negation words, and intensity words) trained only with sentence-level annotations capture linguistic sentiment-shifting phenomena and improve sentence-level sentiment classification performance?
main_claims: Introducing linguistically inspired regularizers (non-sentiment, sentiment, negation, intensity) into LSTM/Bi-LSTM yields improved sentence-level sentiment classification compared to vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM baselines.

The proposed LR-LSTM and LR-Bi-LSTM achieve performance comparable to or slightly better than tree-structured models (e.g., Tree-LSTM) while avoiding dependency on parsing trees and phrase-level annotation.

Negation- and intensity-specific transformation parameters capture diverse, word-specific sentiment-shifting behaviors (evidence shown via distribution-shift visualizations and confusion-matrix style analyses).
Non-sentiment and sentiment regularizers contribute most to overall gains, while negation and intensity regularizers provide larger gains on subsets containing negators/intensifiers.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Classification accuracy on standard benchmarks (MR, SST) compared to baseline neural models (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, Tree-LSTM, CNN, etc.).
Ablation studies measuring the individual contribution of each regularizer (NSR, SR, NR, IR).
Analysis of learned transformation parameters showing whether negation/intensity matrices produce linguistically plausible shifts (e.g., polarity reversal, intensity amplification).
Robustness to training annotation level (performance when trained only with sentence-level annotation vs. models that use phrase-level supervision).
Coverage and quality of external linguistic resources (lexicon, negator/intensifier lists) and their impact on results.
Statistical significance of reported improvements and sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., regularization weight α, margin M).
Computational/efficiency considerations relative to tree-based models (training/inference cost and model complexity).

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Adjacent-position predicted sentiment distributions should be similar when the intervening word is non-opinion (NSR assumption).
supporting_evidence: Sec 4: "Non-Sentiment Regularizer: if the two adjacent positions are all non-opinion words, the sentiment distributions of the two positions should be close to each other."
Formalized as L(NSR)t = max(0, DKL(pt||pt-1) - M).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If non-opinion adjacent words frequently alter sentiment distribution (e.g., compositional idioms, domain-specific collocations), NSR could bias the model towards underfitting local sentiment shifts and degrade classification or obscure true sentiment-carrying patterns.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Sentiment words listed in the combined lexicon reliably indicate prior polarity classes usable for a shared class-specific shifting distribution (SR assumption).
supporting_evidence: Sec 4.2 defines a class-specific shifting distribution sc for each sentiment class in the lexicon; words of same class share sc.
Sec 5.1 describes lexicon combined from MPQA and SST leaf nodes producing 9,750 words with 4 sentiment labels.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If lexicon labels are noisy, ambiguous, or not granular enough, shared shifting vectors may be incorrect, causing wrong regularization signals and harming learning; domain mismatch could reduce utility.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Negation and intensity effects can be approximated by word-specific linear transformations (matrices) applied to neighboring predicted label distributions, without explicit negation/intensity scope resolution.
supporting_evidence: Sec 4.3: propose Txj ∈ R^{C×C} for each negation word m and use softmax(Txj × pt-1) (Eq.9).
Sec 4.5: minimize distance to transformed forward/backward distributions to partially address unknown scope.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the effect of negators/intensifiers depends on syntactic scope, long-distance dependencies, or semantic type of target phrases, a local linear transform may misrepresent real shifts, reducing effectiveness on cases where scope matters.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Sequence LSTMs (possibly bidirectional) can encode enough context about modification targets so that neighboring-state regularization (based on ht) suffices to capture sentiment-shifting effects without explicit scope labeling.
supporting_evidence: Sec 4: "Note that in sequence models, the hidden state of the current position also encodes forward or backward contexts."
Sec 4.5: use Bi-LSTM and minimization operator to let model determine which side to choose.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If ht does not reliably encode the exact modified token(s) (e.g., due to long-range dependencies or model capacity limits), regularizers tied to adjacent hidden states may apply transformations to wrong targets or be weak, reducing effectiveness.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes augmenting sequence LSTM/Bi-LSTM models with four linguistically motivated regularizers (Non-Sentiment, Sentiment, Negation, Intensity) that penalize/supply constraints on adjacent-position predicted sentiment distributions. The rationale: lexicon entries provide priors and negators/intensifiers systematically shift distributions, so adding margin-based symmetric-KL penalties (with learned class shift vectors and word-specific transformation matrices) will teach sequence models to exhibit linguistically plausible distributional shifts despite training only on sentence-level labels. Empirically, the authors report improved accuracies over vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM on MR and SST, ablations showing NSR/SR contribute most globally while NR/IR help targeted subsets, and visual/aggregate diagnostics (scatter plots and transition counts) suggesting learned transformations produce diverse negation/intensification effects. The argument chain is coherent in broad strokes (motivation → formalization → implementation → experiments → analysis), but several links are weak: comparisons mix supervision regimes and reprinted vs re-implemented baselines, variance/significance is not reported, lexicon/negator coverage and per-word data sparsity are not quantified, and the approximation of scope via local adjacent-state regularizers (and Bi-LSTM min heuristic) is hand-waved rather than empirically tested on scope-challenging cases. Overall, the method is plausible and likely useful as a lightweight, linguistically informed enhancement for sequence models, but robustness, calibration, and fair baseline comparisons require strengthening to fully substantiate the stronger empirical and interpretability claims.
logical_argument_graph: Motivation: Tree-structured models perform well but require parsing and phrase-level annotation; sequence LSTMs are simpler but underutilize linguistic resources (lexicons, negators, intensifiers).
Hypothesis: Injecting linguistically informed constraints on local predicted label distributions can make sequence LSTMs capture sentiment-shifting phenomena without phrase-level supervision.

Design: Define four regularizers operating on adjacent predicted distributions (NSR: keep distributions similar for non-opinion adjacent tokens; SR: add learned class shift vector for lexicon entries; NR/IR: learn word-specific C×C transforms and compare transformed neighbor distributions with current position), plugged into overall loss with weighting α and hinge margin M using symmetric KL.

Implementation choice: Use LSTM/Bi-LSTM hidden states to produce position-wise predicted distributions; apply transforms to forward/backward neighbor distributions and use min operator in Bi-LSTM to approximate unknown modification direction/scope.
Claimed consequence 1: LR-LSTM/LR-Bi-LSTM outperform vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM on standard sentence-level sentiment tasks (MR, SST) when trained with sentence-level supervision.
Claimed consequence 2: Performance is comparable to tree-structured models (Tree-LSTM) while avoiding parsing and phrase labels; therefore method is simpler and more efficient.
Claimed consequence 3: Ablation shows NSR and SR provide the bulk of dataset-level gains; NR/IR produce larger gains on negation/intensifier subsets.
Claimed consequence 4: Learned negation/intensity matrices capture diverse, linguistically plausible shifts (visualized scatter and transition-count matrices).

Caveat chain: Regularizers rely on assumptions (lexicon accuracy, adjacent-state encoding of target, sufficiency of linear transforms, margin calibration); these assumptions are acknowledged but not fully empirically stress-tested (e.g., scope complexity, lexicon perturbation, statistical variance).

Recommendation path (implicit): The approach is promising; confirmatory experiments suggested include matched-supervision baseline re-runs, multiple-runs reporting, lexicon sensitivity analyses, and quantitative metrics for transform interpretability.

strengths.title: Clear, linguistically motivated formalization
strengths.description: The paper maps intuitive linguistic phenomena (non-opinion adjacency, lexical prior, negation, intensification) to concrete, learnable regularizers operating on adjacent predicted distributions, which is both conceptually clean and implementable within standard sequence models.
evidence: Section 4: explicit definitions of NSR, SR, NR, IR with equations (Eq.5-14).
Use of symmetric KL margin hinge provides a unified penalty formulation across phenomena.

strengths.title: Practical objective that preserves sentence-level supervision
strengths.description: The method avoids requiring phrase-level annotation or parsing while attempting to induce linguistically plausible behavior via loss-level constraints, aligning with the stated goal of simplicity and applicability to real-world data.
evidence: Section 1 and 5.1: explicit claim and experimental setup that only sentence-level labels are used.
Reported improvements over vanilla LSTMs in Table 3.

strengths.title: Targeted ablation and diagnostic analyses
strengths.description: Paper includes ablation studies (per-regularizer removal) and focused subset evaluations (negation/intensity subsets) plus visualization/transition analyses that move beyond single-number reporting towards process-level interpretability.
evidence: Tables 4 and 5: ablation and subset results.
Figures 1 and 2: visualization of negation and intensifier effects.

concerns.title: Mixed/unequal baseline comparisons
concerns.description: Reported comparisons mix reprinted numbers (possibly different supervision regimes and hyperparameters) with reimplemented results; some baselines use phrase-level supervision while LR models use sentence-level only, making parity claims ambiguous.
evidence: Table 3 notes: '*' (re-printed) vs '#' (own implementation); discussion compares LR sentence-only numbers to Tree-LSTM phrase-level numbers.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-run key baselines (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, Tree-LSTM) under identical data splits, training regimes, and hyperparameter search; present paired comparisons stratified by supervision level (sentence-only vs phrase-level).

concerns.title: Lack of variability and statistical testing
concerns.description: All reported accuracies are single numbers without error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests—this makes it hard to know whether reported improvements exceed run-to-run variability.
evidence: Tables 3, 4, 5 present single accuracy values with no standard deviation or p-values.
Shared analysis flagged absence of significance reporting.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report mean and standard deviation across multiple random seeds (e.g., 5-10 runs) for all main comparisons and ablations; perform significance testing (paired t-test or bootstrap) for claimed improvements.

concerns.title: Approximate handling of negation/intensity scope
concerns.description: The method avoids explicit scope modeling and relies on adjacent-position distributions plus a Bi-LSTM min heuristic; scope complexity is acknowledged but not empirically probed, leaving open the possibility of systematic failure on long-range or syntactically complex scopes.
evidence: Section 4.5: explicit statement that modification span is not considered and that a minimization operator plus Bi-LSTM is used as a heuristic.
Shared analysis notes scope handling may fail when target is non-local.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include diagnostic tests on sentences with known long-distance negation/intensifier scope (manually curated or labeled subset); report performance breakdown by syntactic distance between negator/intensifier and sentiment-bearing token.

concerns.title: Lexicon and negator/intensifier coverage and sparsity
concerns.description: Although the lexicon is large (9,750 entries) and negators/intensifiers were manually collected, the coverage per dataset and per-word frequency distribution isn't quantified; low-frequency negators/intensifiers could lead to poorly estimated per-word matrices.
evidence: Section 5.1 reports total counts of sentences containing sentiment/negation/intensity words but not per-word frequency distributions.
Shared analysis indicates some negation/intensifier counts are small (14%/23% sentence coverage).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide per-word frequency histograms for negators/intensifiers and lexicon words; conduct sensitivity experiments where low-frequency transformation matrices are tied/shared (e.g., cluster-based or class-level transforms) and report differences.

concerns.title: Interpretability analyses are descriptive not quantitative
concerns.description: Visualizations (scatter, transition matrices) are helpful but lack quantitative measures (e.g., polarity flip rates, correlation with hand-labeled expectations, matrix norm statistics) to substantiate claims that learned transforms are linguistically plausible.
evidence: Sections 5.4 and 5.5 use plots and counts but do not report quantitative alignment with gold linguistic expectations.
Shared analysis recommends quantitative probe metrics but none are present.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute and report metrics: per-negator polarity flip rate, average KL shift conditional on input polarity bins, correlation between transform-induced label changes and manually assigned expected shifts; include examples of failure modes.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter/margin calibration sensitivity
concerns.description: The regularizers rely on margin M and weight α (and possibly per-regularizer scaling) but the paper does not present sensitivity analyses showing robustness to these choices.
evidence: Section 4 uses hinge with margin M and weighting α in Eq.4 but implementation details and sensitivity not described (supplementary file referenced).

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include a short hyperparameter sweep (or ablation) showing performance variation with α and M and report recommended default ranges; if training is sensitive, discuss calibration procedure.

uncertainty_flags: Main reported numeric gains lack variance/error bars—uncertain whether improvement is robust across seeds.
Baseline parity: mixing reprinted and reimplemented numbers risks incomparable settings.

alternative_interpretations: Improvements could primarily stem from effective regularization that reduces overfitting rather than from faithful linguistic modeling—NSR/SR may act as smoothing priors that help any sequence model.

NR/IR gains on targeted subsets might come from having additional parameters that incidentally fit frequent local patterns rather than from correctly modeling scope or semantics; per-word matrices may memorize common collocations.

Comparable performance to Tree-LSTM could reflect differences in supervision (sentence-only vs phrase-level) rather than an intrinsic modeling parity; Tree-LSTM may simply be disadvantaged when phrase labels are withheld.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The particular combination of adjacent-distribution regularization with learnable per-word C×C transforms is not a close replica of prominent prior works; this uniqueness signals innovation but does not guarantee empirical validity—robustness and fair comparisons must be demonstrated.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If lexicon labels align well with dataset vocabulary and frequent negators/intensifiers have enough training occurrences, learned transforms will be well-estimated and produce stable improvements.
If symmetric-KL margin regularization is calibrated (α, M tuned) to balance supervision and linguistic constraints, the method can improve generalization rather than overconstrain.

If Bi-LSTM hidden states reliably encode modification targets in adjacent positions (i.e., local syntactic patterns dominate), the adjacent-distribution approach suffices; else explicit scope modeling will be necessary.
If baseline re-implementations under identical settings preserve the reported gaps, then the approach provides a practical lightweight alternative to tree-based models.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The work composes known elements (lexicons, LSTMs, margin-based KL penalties) into a concrete, implementable regularization scheme; incremental but practical.
evidence: Use of MPQA + SST lexicon, LSTMs, and margin-based KL hinge is not radical; the novelty lies in combining them into adjacency regularizers with per-word transforms.
uncertainty_flags: Degree of innovation depends on baselines and whether comparable prior neural lexicon-integration methods (e.g., Teng et al.) were tuned similarly.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes adding four linguistically motivated regularizers to sequence LSTM/Bi-LSTM models for sentence-level sentiment classification: Non-Sentiment Regularizer (NSR), Sentiment Regularizer (SR), Negation Regularizer (NR), and Intensity Regularizer (IR). Each regularizer penalizes (via a margin-based symmetric KL divergence) deviations between the predicted label distribution at position t and transformed distributions of adjacent positions. SR uses class-specific additive "shifting" distributions for lexicon entries; NR and IR use learned word-specific C×C transformation matrices applied to adjacent-position predicted distributions (softmax(T × p)). The full objective augments cross-entropy with α-weighted regularization terms. Bi-LSTM is used with a min heuristic (min distance to forward/backward transformed neighbor) to handle unknown modifier direction/scope. Experiments on MR (binary) and SST (5-way) show consistent improvements of LR-LSTM / LR-Bi-LSTM over vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM and reported numbers claimed comparable to tree-based models that rely on phrase-level supervision. Ablations indicate NSR and SR drive most dataset-level gains, while NR/IR give larger gains on subsets containing negators/intensifiers. Visualization and aggregate counts are used to argue that learned transformation parameters capture diverse, word-specific sentiment-shifting behaviors. The main methodological dependencies for the results to hold are: (1) quality and coverage of the lexicon and the manually collected negator/intensifier lists, (2) calibration and robustness of margin/α hyperparameters, (3) sufficiency of adjacent hidden states as proxies for modification targets (scope), and (4) stability across random seeds and training settings. Evidence is partial: numerical improvements are reported but variance/statistical significance, hyperparameter sensitivity, lexicon sensitivity, computational cost, and detailed quantitative diagnostics of learned matrices are missing or referenced to supplementary material not shown.
logical_argument_graph: If adjacent hidden states in LSTM encode sufficient contextual information about nearby content, then regularizing adjacent predicted label distributions can inject linguistic priors without needing phrase-level supervision.
NSR constrains non-opinion words to keep distributions similar -> reduces spurious fluctuations and encourages local smoothness.

SR uses lexicon-derived class shifts so encountering a sentiment word should cause a predictable distributional drift -> encourages the model to align hidden representations with known polarity priors.

NR/IR model word-specific transformation matrices applied to neighboring distributions -> can model diverse shifter behaviors (reversal, neutralization, amplification) if matrices are learned from sufficient examples.
Bi-LSTM + min heuristic approximates unknown modifier direction, allowing NR/IR to apply even without explicit scope resolution.
Combined, these regularizers guide sequence LSTMs to better approximate compositional sentiment phenomena, improving sentence-level classification when trained with sentence-level labels only.

concerns.title: Potential overfitting on low-frequency modifier words

If per-word transformation matrices are regularized or shared for low-frequency modifiers (or low-rank factored), the model can avoid overfitting and demonstrate transferability to out-of-domain examples.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes to augment simple sequence LSTM/Bi-LSTM sentence classifiers with four linguistically-motivated regularizers that operate on adjacent-position predicted sentiment distributions: (1) Non-Sentiment Regularizer (NSR) to keep distributions similar across non-opinion adjacent tokens; (2) Sentiment Regularizer (SR) that adds a class-specific shifting distribution for lexicon-identified sentiment words; (3) Negation Regularizer (NR) that applies a learned word-specific C×C linear transform (followed by softmax) to model negators' effect; and (4) Intensity Regularizer (IR) similarly for intensifiers. These are integrated as hinge-style symmetric KL penalties in the loss (Eq.4) weighted by α and using margin M. For Bi-LSTM the paper uses a min heuristic between forward/backward transformed neighbor distributions to sidestep explicit scope resolution. Empirically, the authors report consistent accuracy gains over vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM on MR and SST (Tables 3–5), show that NSR/SR provide the largest dataset-level improvements while NR/IR give targeted gains on negation/intensity subsets, and visualize learned transformations (Figures 1–2) to argue interpretability (polarity flips, neutralization, amplification). The paper positions itself as an engineering+linguistically-informed incremental contribution: it aims to recover some of the benefits of tree-structured, phrase-supervised models without requiring parse trees or phrase labels by imposing lightweight linguistic constraints during sentence-level training.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Neural LSTMs can encode local context in hidden states but do not explicitly enforce linguistic shifting behavior (Section 3).
P2: Linguistic phenomena (sentiment-bearing words, negators, intensifiers) systematically affect sentiment distributions of nearby tokens (Section 4 motivation).
M1: Formalize these phenomena as penalties on adjacent-position predicted label distributions (Eq.4–14): NSR, SR, NR, IR using symmetric KL hinge and learned parameters (sc vectors, Tm matrices).
M2: Apply regularizers during sentence-level supervised training (no phrase-level labels), optionally using Bi-LSTM and min heuristic to handle unknown directionality (Section 4.5).
E1: Empirical gains over vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM on MR and SST (Table 3) and substantial ablation effects showing NSR/SR are most important globally while NR/IR matter on relevant subsets (Tables 4,5).
E2: Visualizations/transition matrices show learned per-negator/per-intensifier transformations produce varied behaviors (Figures 1–2), aligning qualitatively with linguistic expectations.
C1: Therefore, linguistically regularized sequence LSTMs can capture sentiment-shifting phenomena and improve sentence-level classification without phrase-level annotation.

Caveat A: Comparisons are sometimes across differing supervision regimes (phrase-level vs sentence-level) and lack reported variance/statistical tests; lexicon/negator coverage and parameter sparsity may influence gains.

Implication: The method is an incremental but meaningful engineering approach that trades explicit scope/syntax modeling for simple per-word parameterization and a distribution-level regularization objective.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a simple but conceptually distinct way to inject linguistic knowledge into sequence LSTM models by adding distributional regularizers on adjacent token-level predicted label distributions. Four regularizers are defined: Non-Sentiment Regularizer (NSR) enforcing small symmetric-KL drift across adjacent non-opinion tokens; Sentiment Regularizer (SR) applying a learned class-specific label-shift vector sc for lexicon-identified sentiment words; Negation Regularizer (NR) and Intensity Regularizer (IR) that apply learned word-specific C×C transformation matrices to neighboring predicted label distributions and use hinge-margin symmetric KL losses to enforce transformed-neighbor ≈ current prediction. For Bi-LSTM the model computes forward/backward transformed neighbors and takes a min-distance heuristic to cope with unknown modifier direction. Training uses only sentence-level cross-entropy plus α-weighted sum of regularizer terms (and L2). Empirically, LR-LSTM and LR-Bi-LSTM beat vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM on MR and SST (Table 3), show ablation evidence that NSR and SR yield most dataset-level gains while NR/IR give larger gains on negation/intensity-containing subsets (Tables 4–5), and produce visualization/aggregate diagnostics indicating diverse learned negator/intensifier behaviors (Figures 1–2). Key methodological omissions: no multi-seed variances or tests of statistical significance, limited quantitative validation of learned transforms beyond plotted examples, incomplete reporting of hyperparameter search and resource lists (supplementary file referenced), and no measured computational cost for per-word matrices. Conceptually, the paper frames linguistic phenomena as soft constraints on model outputs (label distributions) rather than hard features or tree-based composition rules, which is an under-explored framing and potentially generative for other tasks.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Sequence LSTMs encode contextual information in hidden states ht, so pt (softmax over ht) approximates local predicted sentiment distributions.

A2: Linguistic observations: (i) non-opinion neighbors should not change predicted distributions much; (ii) sentiment words cause distributional drift toward class-specific shifts; (iii) negators/intensifiers cause word-specific, potentially non-symmetric shifts.

Design: Implement NSR, SR, NR, IR as margin-based symmetric-KL penalties between pt and transformed neighbor distributions (Eq.5–14) to softly impose A2 constraints while training only with sentence-level supervision.
Optimization: Minimize standard cross-entropy + α*sum_regularizers + L2, learning sc vectors and word-specific Tx matrices jointly with LSTM parameters.
Bi-LSTM heuristic: compute forward/backward transformed neighbors and take the min hinge-distance to handle unknown direction/scope (Eq.14).
Empirical claim: Gains over vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM on MR and SST show regularizers produce measurable improvement (Table 3).
Ablation: Removing NSR/SR drops dataset-level accuracy more than removing NR/IR; on negation/intensity subsets NR/IR removal causes larger drops (Tables 4–5).
Interpretation: Visualizations (Figures 1–2) show learned transforms produce polarity reversal, neutralization, amplification — supporting linguistic plausibility of learned parameters.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes augmenting sequence LSTM and Bi-LSTM sentence classifiers with four linguistically motivated regularizers (Non-Sentiment NSR, Sentiment SR, Negation NR, Intensity IR). Each regularizer imposes hinge-margin symmetric-KL penalties between the predicted label distribution at a token and either an adjacent token's distribution (NSR), an adjacent distribution shifted by a class-specific vector for lexicon entries (SR), or an adjacent distribution transformed by a learned word-specific C×C matrix for negators/intensifiers (NR/IR). For Bi-LSTM they use a min heuristic over forward/backward neighbors to approximate unknown modifier direction/scope. Experiments on MR (binary) and SST (5-way) report consistent gains of LR-LSTM/LR-Bi-LSTM over vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM (e.g., MR: 81.5 vs 77.4; LR-Bi-LSTM 82.1 vs Bi-LSTM 79.3). Ablations show NSR/SR drive most dataset-level gains; NR/IR yield larger gains on subsets containing negators/intensifiers. Visual diagnostics (scatter plots and transition-count matrices) are used to argue that learned transforms capture varied negation/intensifier behaviors. The evidence in the manuscript supports the plausibility and practical effectiveness of the regularizers under the reported settings, but several empirical and methodological gaps reduce confidence in generality and strength of interpretability claims: baseline comparability across supervision regimes is mixed, no variance/significance testing is shown, lexicon/negator list coverage and per-word frequency effects are underreported, and the heuristic scope-handling (adjacent hidden states + Bi-LSTM min) is untested on syntactically complex or long-distance modification cases. I mark specific claims as supported, partially supported, or overstated in the identified_claims below and propose concrete follow-ups to strengthen the manuscript.
logical_argument_graph: Motivation: Tree-structured models need parse trees/phrase labels; linguistic phenomena (sentiment lexicon, negators, intensifiers) are important but underused in sequence models.

Design: Add four regularizers (NSR, SR, NR, IR) as hinge-margin symmetric-KL penalties between token-level predicted distributions and transformed adjacent distributions (shift vectors or per-word matrices).
Training: Train LSTM/Bi-LSTM with sentence-level cross-entropy augmented by α-weighted regularizers; Bi-LSTM uses min-of-forward-and-backward distances to approximate scope.
Empirical claim 1: LR-LSTM / LR-Bi-LSTM yield higher sentence-level accuracy than vanilla LSTM / Bi-LSTM on MR and SST.
Empirical claim 2: Performance is comparable to some tree-structured models without requiring parse trees or phrase-level annotation.
Ablation claim: NSR and SR contribute most to overall dataset-level gains; NR and IR give larger gains on negation/intensity subsets.

Interpretability claim: Learned per-word transformations (NR/IR) produce diverse and linguistically plausible shifts (reversal, neutralization, amplification) evidenced by scatter and transition matrices.
Caveats/assumptions: Lexicon quality/coverage, choice of margin/α, frequency of modifier words, and heuristic scope handling are critical for claims to hold robustly.

strengths.title: Linguistically motivated, modular regularizers
strengths.description: The four regularizers are clearly derived from linguistic observations (non-opinion adjacency, lexicon priors, negation, intensity) and map cleanly to mathematical penalties on token-level label distributions.
evidence: Section 4 formalizes NSR, SR, NR, IR (Eq.5-14) with explicit formulas and parameters (sc vectors, Tx matrices).
Discussion in Section 4.6 explains motivation for class-specific shifts and word-specific negator/intensifier transforms.

strengths.title: Practical aim: sentence-only supervision
strengths.description: Method targets a realistic constraint—avoiding phrase-level annotation—offering a low-friction way to inject linguistic knowledge into sequence models.
evidence: Introduction and experimental setup explicitly state models are trained with sentence-level annotations only.
Reported results show gains over vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM without requiring phrase labels.

strengths.title: Targeted ablation and subset analyses
strengths.description: The manuscript includes sensible ablation studies and focused subset evaluations that reveal which regularizers drive global vs targeted gains.
evidence: Tables 4 and 5 present ablation on each regularizer and performance on negation/intensity-containing subsets.
Authors discuss that NSR/SR dominate dataset-level improvements while NR/IR help targeted cases.

strengths.title: Interpretability-oriented diagnostics
strengths.description: Visualizations (scatter plots and transition matrices) provide qualitative evidence that learned transforms produce varied linguistic effects (polarity flips, neutralization, intensity shifts).
evidence: Section 5.4 (Figure 1) shows positive-score before/after negation scatter; Section 5.5 (Figure 2) shows intensifier transition matrices.
Textual examples are given in discussion of plots.

concerns.title: Lack of statistical reporting and run-level variance
concerns.description: Results are presented as single-point accuracies without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, limiting assessment of robustness across seeds and training variability.
evidence: Tables 3–5 show single accuracy numbers with no reported variance.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers note absence of multiple-seed averages and statistical tests.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run each key experiment (main comparisons and ablations) with multiple random seeds (e.g., 5–10), report mean ± std, and perform appropriate significance tests (e.g., paired bootstrap or t-test) when comparing LR vs baselines.

concerns.title: Mixed baseline provenance and supervision mismatch
concerns.description: Comparisons mix reprinted numbers and in-house reimplementations and conflate phrase-level and sentence-level supervision in cross-model comparisons; this complicates claims of parity with tree-structured models.
evidence: Table 3 marks some results as re-printed (*) and others as reimplemented (#).
Phrase-level Tree-LSTM numbers are compared against sentence-level LR models without fully matched supervision.
Prior-stage digest flags baseline parity concern.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-run baselines (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, Tree-LSTM) under identical data splits, preprocessing, optimization/hyperparameter search and supervision level (sentence-only vs phrase-level), or clearly separate comparisons by supervision regime.

concerns.title: Underspecified lexicon and modifier resource coverage
concerns.description: The combined lexicon and manually collected negator/intensifier lists are described at a high level (MPQA + SST leaves; manual lists) but lack per-word frequencies, selection criteria, and sensitivity analyses; sparse counts for modifier words may underdetermine per-word Tx matrices.
evidence: Section 5.1 describes lexicon composition (9,750 words) and manual negator/intensifier lists but defers full lists to supplementary material.
Table 1 reports only counts of sentences containing any sentiment, negation, intensity words, not per-word counts.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide the full lists and per-word frequency statistics in the supplement; run sensitivity experiments that ablate or perturb lexicon/modifier entries and group low-frequency words to test stability of learned transforms (or tie parameters for rare words).

concerns.title: Heuristic handling of negation/intensity scope
concerns.description: The model does not explicitly resolve modification scope; it relies on adjacent hidden-state regularization and a Bi-LSTM min heuristic, which may fail for long-distance or syntactically complex scopes.
evidence: Section 4.3-4.5 acknowledge they do not model modification span and use min-of-forward/backward distances as an approximation (Eq.11, Eq.14).
Prior reviewers flagged scope-handling as a central assumption risk (A3, A4, A8).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate on targeted test cases where negation/intensifier scope is non-local or syntactically complex (manually curated examples or annotated scope corpora); report degradation cases and consider simple scope-aware heuristics (e.g., dependency distance threshold) or soft attention to better localize targets.

concerns.title: Interpretability claims are qualitative
concerns.description: Evidence that learned Tx matrices and sc vectors correspond to linguistically expected transformations is largely qualitative (plots, exemplar phrases); no quantitative alignment with human annotations, polarity-flip rates, or matrix diagnostics is presented.
evidence: Sections 5.4 and 5.5 provide scatter plots and count matrices but no metrics like percent polarity flip, correlation with hand-labeled shifts, or per-word confidence based on frequency.
Shared analysis recommends quantitative probing of transforms.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute quantitative diagnostics: per-negator polarity-flip rate, average change in predicted class probability mass, correlation with hand-labeled expectations (if available), and condition these metrics on per-word frequency; present representative Tx matrices (heatmaps) alongside norms and entropy measures.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter sensitivity and calibration missing
concerns.description: The choice of regularizer weight α and margin M affects the hinge KL penalties; manuscript lacks systematic sensitivity analysis and guidance for reproducibility.
evidence: Eq.4 uses α and Eq.5/others use margin M; text refers to supplementary implementation details but main text doesn't report sensitivity.
Prior-stage notes call out need for hyperparameter sensitivity checks.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report hyperparameter ranges, selected values, and ablation/sensitivity plots showing performance vs α and M; include training curves demonstrating stability and any early-stopping criteria.

concerns.title: Computational cost and parameter overhead not reported
concerns.description: Per-word C×C transformation matrices introduce parameters proportional to number of modifier words; no account of parameter counts, memory/training time overhead, or comparison to Tree-LSTM efficiency is provided.
evidence: Section 4.3 notes m matrices for m negation words; no parameter counts or runtimes are shown.
Paper claims simplicity/efficiency vs tree models but provides no quantitative cost comparisons.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide parameter counts attributable to regularizers, training/inference time comparisons (wall-clock) with LSTM/Bi-LSTM and Tree-LSTM, and describe any regularization/tie strategies used for low-frequency words (e.g., shared transforms).

uncertainty_flags: Main numeric results are single-run point estimates without reported variance or significance.
Baseline numbers mix reprinted and reimplemented results; supervision-level (phrase vs sentence) is not always matched.
Per-word frequency and coverage of negator/intensifier lists are not presented; learned per-word matrices may be underdetermined for rare words.
Scope-resolution is not modeled; approximation via adjacent hidden states and Bi-LSTM min heuristic may fail on long-range or syntactically complex cases.
Supplementary material containing implementation details is referenced but not provided here; reproduction may hinge on those details.
alternative_interpretations: Gains attributed to linguistic regularizers could partly arise from additional parameterization or implicit smoothing effect rather than explicit linguistic modeling. For example, adding per-word transforms increases model capacity and may regularize gradients or act as a form of label smoothing.

The apparent parity with tree-structured models may be due to comparing different supervision regimes (LR trained with sentence-level labels vs tree models with phrase-level labels); when supervision is matched, differences may shrink or reverse.
Visualized distributional shifts may reflect model overfitting on modifier-containing training examples for frequent negators/intensifiers; rare modifiers' behavior might be unreliable.
transparency_notes: Full lists of lexicon entries and negator/intensifier words are deferred to supplementary material but are necessary to assess coverage and reproducibility.

Details about random seeds, hyperparameter search ranges (α, margin M), optimizer settings, and convergence criteria are referenced but not available in the provided excerpts—these should be included in the supplement or main text.
Baseline reimplementations should include code or configuration details to allow exact replication; mark which baselines were reimplemented and how hyperparameters were chosen.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper's framing—imposing linguistically motivated output-distribution regularizers at token-level rather than changing internal composition functions—has limited close analogs in the retrieved literature, which typically use lexicon features, specialized composition functions, or tree structures. Sparse precedent suggests potential innovation but does not guarantee empirical robustness; empirical rigor is needed to separate novelty from fragility.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If lexicon and modifier lists have high coverage and frequent occurrences in training data, learned per-word transforms will be well-estimated and likely capture modifier-specific effects.

If regularizer hyperparameters (α, M) are tuned and produce moderate constraints (not over- or under-regularizing), the approach will nudge sequence models toward linguistically-plausible outputs without harming learning.
If most sentiment shifts are local (modifier and target close in linear order) so adjacent hidden states reliably encode targets, the adjacent-position regularizers will be effective.
If multiple training seeds show stable gains, the approach will be robust and likely generalize; conversely, if gains vanish across seeds, the method's impact is fragile.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The method integrates known ingredients—lexicons, negation/intensifier modeling—into sequence LSTMs via a new regularization formulation. This is a clear engineering contribution that makes linguistic signals usable with sentence-level supervision.
evidence: Formulation of NSR/SR/NR/IR as hinge-margin symmetric-KL penalties (Eq.5-14).
Empirical ablation showing targeted improvements.
uncertainty_flags: Comparability with prior work is muddied by supervision-level mismatches and lack of multi-seed robustness checks.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Framing linguistic phenomena as soft constraints on predicted label distributions is an under-explored methodological angle that could generalize to other structured-label tasks (e.g., modality, factuality) and to other architectures.
evidence: Section 4 formalizes distributional regularizers independent of internal representation choices.
Discussion suggests applying regularizers to tree-LSTM as future work.
uncertainty_flags: Empirical validation across more datasets and robust statistical reporting is needed to confirm generalizability.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident that the main qualitative conclusions are correct (regularizers can improve sequence LSTMs and learned transforms show varied behaviors), but the quantitative strength and generality of the results are uncertain due to lack of multi-seed reporting, baseline parity issues, and underspecified resource and hyperparameter sensitivity. The interval reflects moderate-to-high epistemic uncertainty that should be resolved by the suggested experiments.

consensus_findings: The paper presents a coherent, implementable set of linguistically-motivated regularizers (NSR, SR, NR, IR) that are formally defined as margin-based symmetric-KL penalties on adjacent token-level predicted label distributions and can be integrated into LSTM/Bi-LSTM training.

Across the reported experiments on MR and SST, LR-LSTM and LR-Bi-LSTM show consistent point-estimate improvements over the authors' vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM baselines and ablative patterns indicate NSR and SR drive most dataset-level gains while NR and IR provide targeted gains on negation/intensifier-containing subsets.

The paper provides qualitative interpretability diagnostics (scatter plots, label-transition matrices, example phrases) indicating the learned negator/intensifier parameters exhibit diverse behaviors (polarity reversal, neutralization, amplification) rather than a single uniform transform.

The authors aim to avoid phrase-level supervision and parsing-dependence; they explicitly train only with sentence-level labels and position this as a practical advantage relative to tree-structured models that rely on phrase annotations.
disagreements: Degree of empirical support for parity with tree-structured models: several reviewers flagged that comparisons mix phrase-level and sentence-level baselines (reprinted vs reimplemented), so whether LR models are truly 'comparable' to tree models under matched supervision is contested.

Interpretability sufficiency: reviewers agree learned transforms show varied behaviors qualitatively, but disagree on whether the provided visualizations are sufficient evidence of linguistically faithful modeling—some view visuals as promising illustrative evidence, others want quantitative alignment metrics.

Source of performance gains: some reviewers propose that gains mainly come from generic smoothing/regularization or lexicon priors (SR/NSR) rather than correct modeling of negation/intensification; others accept that NR/IR plausibly contribute on targeted subsets but caution about overfitting for low-frequency modifiers.

Novelty framing: reviewers differ in labeling the contribution as incremental engineering versus a conceptually novel framing (treating linguistic phenomena as soft constraints on output distributions). Some call it a modest but useful engineering contribution; a minority emphasize conceptual novelty but request broader validation.
uncertainty_hotspots: Baseline parity and reproducibility: mixed provenance of baseline numbers (reprinted vs reimplemented) and unclear hyperparameter/matching details create uncertainty whether reported gaps persist under strictly controlled, identical-training conditions.

Statistical robustness: main reported accuracies and ablations are single-run point estimates without multi-seed averages, standard deviations, or statistical tests; effect-size reliability is therefore uncertain.

Lexicon and modifier resource coverage: the combined lexicon and manually collected negator/intensifier lists lack per-word frequency distributions and provenance in the main excerpts; low-frequency modifiers may render per-word matrices underdetermined.

Scope handling: NR/IR rely on adjacent hidden-state transforms and a Bi-LSTM min heuristic rather than explicit scope resolution; performance on long-distance or syntactically complex modifier-target relations is untested and potentially fragile.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: choices of regularizer weight (α) and margin (M), and any per-regularizer scaling, are not systematically reported in the main text excerpts; potential sensitivity to these choices is an open risk.

Parameter/compute overhead: introducing per-word C×C matrices scales parameters with number of modifier words; memory, runtime, and overfitting risks are not quantified and may impact deployment trade-offs.
model_diversity_effects: Role-specific regularizers had differentiated effects: NSR and SR act as broad smoothing/priors benefiting overall dataset-level accuracy, while NR and IR add capacity to model localized shifts and thus produce larger gains on subsets containing negators/intensifiers.

Per-word parameterization (word-specific Tx matrices) increases model expressivity in a way that can capture diverse modifier behaviors but also introduces heterogeneous data requirements across words — frequent modifiers likely yield robust transforms while rare ones risk noisy estimates.

The Bi-LSTM 'min' heuristic introduces a model-architecture dependence: bidirectionality combined with the min operator allows the regularizers to be applied even when modifier directionality is unknown, but this effect may not translate to models without bidirectionality or to longer-range scope cases.

Because NSR/SR supply strong lexical priors, some of the observed improvements could be reproduced by other ways of injecting lexicon knowledge (e.g., lexical features or label-smoothing) — model diversity (choice of regularizer form and parameter-sharing strategy) will influence whether gains are due to linguistic modeling or added inductive bias.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the manuscript as a promising, well-motivated methodological contribution that requires additional empirical rigor before strong claims (e.g., parity with tree-structured models, interpretability of learned transforms) are accepted. Request the authors to (1) provide controlled, apples-to-apples baseline re-runs under identical preprocessing, splits, optimization, and hyperparameter search; (2) report mean and standard deviation across multiple random seeds (≥5) and accompanying statistical tests for main comparisons and ablations; (3) disclose full lexicon and modifier lists and per-word frequency statistics; (4) quantify parameter/compute overhead introduced by per-word matrices and present alternatives (shared/low-rank) if cost is large; and (5) include quantitative diagnostics for learned transforms (e.g., polarity-flip rates, KL-shift summaries, correlation with human expectations). Keep the decision-maker role central: these missing but addressable items should be requested from the authors and reassessed rather than treating current single-run results as conclusive evidence.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and reduce key uncertainties, please (a) re-run key baselines (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, Tree-LSTM) under the exact same experimental pipeline and report results stratified by supervision level (sentence-only vs phrase-level) with full configuration details; (b) run each main experiment and each ablation across multiple random seeds (≥5) and report mean±SD plus significance testing (paired bootstrap or t-tests) for primary comparisons; (c) publish the full lexicon and curated negator/intensifier lists (or a link), provide per-word frequency histograms, and run sensitivity analyses that remove or group low-frequency modifiers and/or tie/share parameters for rare words; (d) quantify computational/parameter overhead (extra parameters due to Tx matrices, training/inference time) and, if necessary, demonstrate compact alternatives (low-rank factorization or clustered transforms) with comparative results; (e) provide quantitative interpretability metrics for learned transforms (e.g., per-negator polarity-flip rate, average KL change conditioned on input polarity bins, correlation with manually specified expected shifts) and report selection/coverage statistics for plotted diagnostic samples; (f) add targeted evaluations for scope complexity: curated cases or an annotated negation-scope subset broken down by linear or dependency distance to the modified target; and (g) disclose exact hyperparameter values and sensitivity analyses for α and margin M. Addressing these points will clarify whether gains are robust, generalize across seeds and domains, and substantiate interpretability claims.
transparency_report: The manuscript provides explicit formal definitions (Eqs.4–14) and ablation tables, and marks baseline provenance (reprinted vs reimplemented) in Table 3 — these are helpful transparency signals.

However, essential reproducibility items are deferred or missing in the provided excerpts: (1) full lexicon and modifier lists and their construction/provenance; (2) per-word frequency counts for lexicon and modifier words; (3) exact hyperparameter settings and search ranges for α, margin M, and any per-regularizer weights; (4) random seeds and number of runs used (none reported in main text excerpts); (5) parameter counts and runtime/memory measurements for model variants; (6) code or configuration to reproduce the diagnostic figures (selection criteria for plotted phrase pairs).

Supplementary material is referenced for implementation details; the reviewers recommend that the supplement or code repository include all of the above to enable full replication and fair baseline comparisons.
epistemic_limits: The synthesis rests on reviewers' readings of manuscript excerpts and shared analysis rather than access to the full supplementary materials or code; therefore conclusions about reproducibility, baseline parity, and hyperparameter sensitivity are provisional. Reported empirical improvements are based on single-run point estimates in the provided text; without multi-seed statistics and controlled reimplementations, it is not possible to determine which observed gains will persist under rigorous replication. Interpretability claims rely primarily on illustrative visualizations and aggregate counts; quantitative alignment with linguistic gold standards or manual annotations is absent in the excerpts, limiting confidence that learned transforms generalize as linguistically-plausible operators rather than dataset-specific patterns. Finally, per-word-parameter estimation reliability (especially for low-frequency modifiers) and the effectiveness of the Bi-LSTM min heuristic for scope remain unresolved until the requested targeted diagnostics and sensitivity analyses are provided.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript defines four linguistically motivated regularizers (Non-Sentiment, Sentiment, Negation, Intensity) that impose margin-based symmetric-KL penalties on adjacent token-level predicted label distributions and integrates them into LSTM/Bi-LSTM training (LR-LSTM / LR-Bi-LSTM). Experiments on MR and SST report consistent point-estimate accuracy gains over vanilla LSTM/Bi-LSTM and ablations indicate NSR/SR drive most global gains while NR/IR provide targeted improvements on negation/intensifier subsets. Qualitative diagnostics (scatter plots, transition-count matrices) are offered as evidence that learned per-word transforms capture diverse modifier behaviors. Reviewers find the idea coherent and practically useful but identify methodological gaps that limit confidence in how robust and general the empirical claims are.
strengths: Clear, linguistically grounded formalization: all four regularizers are precisely defined (Eq.4–14) and map intuitions to implementable loss terms.
Practical focus on sentence-level supervision: method aims to avoid phrase labels and parser reliance, which is attractive for low-resource or deployment settings.
Targeted analyses: per-regularizer ablations and negation/intensifier subset evaluations provide more insight than aggregate scores alone.
Interpretability effort: authors expose learned components (class-shift vectors and per-word C×C transforms) and provide visual/aggregate diagnostics illustrating diverse learned behaviors.
limitations: Single-run reporting and absent statistical testing: main accuracy and ablation numbers are point estimates with no multi-seed means, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests; robustness of reported gains is therefore unknown.

Baseline comparability issues: comparisons mix reprinted and reimplemented baseline numbers and conflate supervision regimes (phrase-level vs sentence-level), so claims of parity with tree-structured models are not demonstrably apples-to-apples.

Underspecified lexical resources and frequency effects: the full lexicon and negator/intensifier lists, per-word occurrence counts, and selection criteria are not presented in the main excerpts; per-word parameter estimation (word-specific Tx matrices) may be unreliable for low-frequency modifiers.

Scope-handling approximation: NR/IR operate via adjacent hidden-state transforms and a Bi-LSTM min heuristic rather than explicit scope resolution; performance on long-distance or syntactically complex scopes is untested and could be fragile.
open_questions: Please report mean ± standard deviation across multiple random seeds (≥5) for all main comparisons and ablations and supply statistical tests (paired bootstrap or other) to indicate which differences are robust.

Provide controlled re-runs of key baselines (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, Tree-LSTM) under identical preprocessing, splits, embedding initialization, optimizer settings, and hyperparameter search so comparisons are strictly matched by supervision regime (sentence-only vs phrase-level).

Release the complete lexicon and negator/intensifier lists (or link), and provide per-word frequency histograms; for low-frequency modifiers, did you apply parameter tying, low-rank factorization, or fallback strategies? Please report sensitivity to grouping/perturbing these lists.

Quantify interpretability claims: compute per-negator polarity-flip rates, average KL shifts conditioned on input polarity bins, and correlation between learned transforms and manual expectations (or a small human-annotated test). What selection criteria and sample sizes underlie Figures 1–2?

Report hyperparameter search details and sensitivity for regularizer weight α and margin M (and any per-regularizer scaling). How sensitive are results to these choices and what defaults are recommended?

Provide parameter/compute accounting: how many additional parameters do per-word C×C matrices add, and what is the wall-clock training/inference overhead relative to baseline LSTM/Bi-LSTM and to Tree-LSTM?
consensus_snapshot: The regularizer framework is conceptually coherent, interpretable, and implementable, mapping linguistic intuitions to distributional penalties.
Authors provide ablation and subset analyses that align with the proposed roles of NSR/SR (global smoothing/prior) and NR/IR (targeted modifier handling).
Qualitative diagnostics indicate learned modifier-specific behaviors are diverse rather than uniform, suggesting the parameterization can capture varied effects.
disagreement_snapshot: Whether reported numeric gains are robust: several reviewers think gains may be within run-to-run variance until multi-seed statistics are provided.
Whether LR models are genuinely 'comparable' to tree-structured models under matched supervision: reviewers disagree because baseline provenance and supervision levels are mixed in the paper.

Interpretability sufficiency: some reviewers view the visualizations as promising evidence of linguistically plausible transforms, while others request quantitative alignment metrics to substantiate interpretability claims.
uncertainty_snapshot: Baseline-provenance uncertainty (reprinted vs reimplemented numbers) makes cross-model parity claims provisional.
Statistical uncertainty due to single-run reporting: effect sizes may shrink or vanish across seeds or with stricter tuning of baselines.
Resource and sampling uncertainty: per-word counts for modifiers are unknown; low-frequency words may lead to noisy per-word matrices and overfitting.

human_facing_meta_review.comments: Summary: The paper proposes an interpretable, linguistically motivated set of regularizers (NSR, SR, NR, IR) that operate on adjacent token-level predicted label distributions and demonstrates point-estimate improvements over vanilla sequence LSTMs with targeted ablation and qualitative diagnostics. Limitations: Results are single-run point estimates with no reported variance or statistical tests; baseline comparisons mix reprinted and reimplemented numbers and conflate supervision regimes; lexicon and modifier resources and per-word frequency statistics are underspecified; scope-handling is heuristic and untested on non-local cases. Transparency: The paper includes formal definitions and notes on baseline provenance, but essential reproducibility artifacts (full lists, seeds, hyperparameter grids, code for diagnostics, parameter counts) must be supplied in supplement or repository. The requested experiments and disclosures are concrete and should materially reduce remaining uncertainties.

top_documents.title: Sentiment Analysis of Short Informal Texts
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: The recursive deep models work in a bottom-top fashion over a parse-tree structure of a sentence to infer the sentiment label of the sentence as a composition of the sentiment expressed by its constituting parts: words and phrases. These models do not require any hand-crafted features or semantic knowledge, such as a list of negation words. However, they are computationally intensive and need substantial additional annotations (word and phrase-level sentiment labeling) to produce competitive results (Socher et al., 2013). In this paper, we propose a simple corpus-based statistical method to estimate the sentiment scores of negated words. As will be shown in Section 6.2.2, this simple method is able to achieve the same level of accuracy as the recursive deep learning approach. Additionally, we analyze the impact of negation on sentiment scores of common sentiment terms.
